newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan steps in to talk up battered dollar.
newsitem.headline: Japan steps in to talk up battered dollar.

text.p: Japan's financial authorities moved to halt a relentless fall of the U.S. currency against the yen in Tokyo trade on Tuesday, warning that the yen's rise was too rapid.
Panic sales during the day had pushed the dollar down more than three yen to 111.98 yen, its lowest level since December, before Japan's top foreign exchange policymaker stepped in to stop the rout.
"The pace of the yen's strengthening is too rapid," Eisuke Sakakibara, the director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, told Reuters.
Sakakibara added that too much volatility in foreign exchange markets was undesirable and that Japan would "deal appropriately" with such excessive volatility.
His comments helped push the dollar back above 113 yen and it was trading at around 113.70 yen at 0930 GMT.

Earlier on Tuesday, Sakakibara told a domestic news agency that the situation was not such that the yen would rise relentlessly and added that he wanted to take steps to keep the sharp rise from hurting Japan's economy.
The dollar has been on a downward spiral ever since hitting a 56-month peak of 127.47 yen on May 1.

Despite the dollar's partial recovery on Sakakibara's verbal intervention, traders were still coming to terms with the consequences of a turnabout in Washington's commitment to a strong dollar and its lack of sympathy for Japan's worries about a steep rise in the yen.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, speaking in New York late on Monday, said U.S. policy on the dollar remained unchanged, but he did not explicitly repeat his past support for a strong dollar.

"People knew that Washington has been wanting a weak dollar against the yen in light of Japan's mushrooming surplus, but they had been unable to face up to the fact," said a chief trader at a major U.S. bank.

That reluctance to recognise the shift in the U.S. stance was partly because many had overbought the dollar over the past several months and partly because Rubin's turn of phrase had been very subtle, perhaps intentionally, the trader added.
Rubin expressed concerns over the ballooning of Japan's surplus, a source of friction between Tokyo and Washington.
"The question is will there be a sustained increase in the current account surplus? And if so I think that is a very serious problem," he said.
His remarks hit the early trading hours in Tokyo on Tuesday and exaggerated the bearish dollar sentiment here.

Japan announced on Monday that its customs-cleared trade surplus grew 163.7 percent to 831.48 billion yen ($7.35 billion) in April and its trade gap with the United States soared 174.1 percent to 468.97 billion yen ($4.15 billion). The data was announced on Monday morning.

The dollar was also battered by expectations of a shrinking interest rate gap between the United States and Japan, given that many market players anticipate that the U.S. Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting later on Tuesday.

This expecation was compounded when Japanese media reported that Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) would recommend later this month that the Bank of Japan raise its official discount rate from a current record-low 0.5 percent to keep capital from flowing out of the country following liberalisation of foreign exchange laws.
An LDP source said later that there had been no decision yet on whether to make such a recommendation, but added that there were calls in the party to do so.

Analysts said the only quick option now available for Japan to avoid a swelling external trade surplus was to strengthen the yen. Another would be drastic deregulation of its economy to boost growth in domestic demand.
